note: Kural 1051 says if those worth asking withhold, the blame is theirs; 196 says a false promise or a false refusal lessens the giver's fame.
teaches: The Kural states as a rule that withholding shames the giver, not the asker, and Avur Moolankizhar applies it to a named king's delay, so the rule had been used as a poet's weapon before it became a maxim.

note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

note: In both the girl looks and bows her head; the Kural takes it as water poured into the bond, while here the bowed head with checked tears leaves the hero in pain.
teaches: The Kural fixes the bowed head as a sign of consent, but the Akananuru shows the same gesture as unreadable to the man at the moment it happens, so the maxim is a reading made after the fact.

note: Thazhumban's Unur stands as the measure of wealth in both, here as the region beyond which the lover's noisy departure is likened to Marungur's market, there as the town a girl's beauty is compared to.
teaches: A chieftain's town famous in puram praise was reused by akam poets as a ready scale of plenty, so a patron's fame circulated as a stock of comparison across the two kinds of poem.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: 186 says the world lives by its king; 187 says a land is good wherever its men are good, naming no king.
teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the two maxims locate the source of a land's well-being in different hands, the ruler in 186 and the men at large in 187, so the reader sees that Sangam counsel did not rest the realm on the king alone.

note: 230 holds death sweet for one who can no longer give. 968 asks whether a life of tending the flesh is any medicine once greatness has lost its dignity (பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து).
teaches: In both a life is not worth keeping once the thing that gave it worth is gone: giving in 230, honour in 968.

note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.

note: In both the evening comes with cold and brings the woman's sorrow to its height.
teaches: The Kural names the evening's chill and the swelling grief in two lines, while the Akananuru supplies the season's things, the north wind, the rain and the flowers, that make the evening cold, so the couplet presupposes the landscape.

note: Akananuru 44 records Pazhaiyan's fall in a war of many chiefs; Akananuru 186 uses Pazhaiyan's town Por on the Kaveri as a likeness for a bangle that will not be broken.
teaches: The same chief appears in one akam poem as a fallen man and in another as the owner of an unbreakable town, so akam poets drew on a chief's fame both before and after his fall.

note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

note: Both say the world stands because of a certain kind of person: 182 names those who strive for others, Kural 996 those of courtesy (பண்புடையார்), without whom it would sink into the earth.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a two-line rule what the Pandya prince builds as a list of concrete refusals, so the reader of the Kural can see which deeds (not eating alone, dying for honour, refusing blame-tainted gain) its abstract பண்பு was taken to mean.

note: 198 has the poet long for the king's grace like the bird that longs for a raindrop; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return daily to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: Both poems make the suppliant a bird, but 198's lone bird waits for a drop and begs not to be forgotten, while 199's flock returns without shame to a sure tree, so the pair shows the bard's two postures, anxious waiting and confident return, and what decides between them is the patron.

note: 192 ends பெரியோரை வியத்தலும் இலமே, we do not marvel at the great; 197 says the poet does not marvel (வியத்தலோ இலமே) at kings' umbrella wealth but at small chiefs who know how to treat poets.
teaches: Kaniyan's refusal to admire the great is a philosophical stance, and Kumaranar turns it into a bard's practice before a king, choosing whom to admire by conduct, so the pair shows a cosmological equanimity becoming a social rule of honour.

note: 1291 opens the chapter with the woman asking her heart why it is not hers when his heart is his own (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). 1300 closes it with the general form: when one's own heart is not one's kin (நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), it is nothing that strangers are not.
teaches: Parimelazhagar gives the first to the woman and the last to the man, so the chapter begins and ends with the same complaint from each side.

note: Both turn on a small child's hand in the food: Kural 64 says gruel stirred by children's small hands is sweeter than nectar; 188 lists the child's touching, biting, stirring and scattering of ghee rice.
teaches: The Kural makes the image a measure of sweetness, while the Pandya king makes its absence a verdict that a rich man's feasting life is profitless, so one scene serves as delight in one book and as the test of a wasted life in the other.

note: Both are the friend's assurance that he will return; 231 grants that glory took him away, 237 says no rich town, not even Uranthai, will keep him from her.
teaches: Taken together the two comforts answer the two fears of the waiting woman, that his honour will keep him away and that pleasure will, and show the friend's arguments as a set repertoire.

note: 742 says a fort has clear water (மணிநீர்), open ground, a hill (மலை) and a forest of fine shade. 737 lists as limbs of a land the two waters (இருபுனல்), a well-placed hill (வாய்ந்த மலை), the water that comes from it, and a strong fort.
teaches: The same features of the terrain, water and hill, are counted first as a land's resources and then as a fort's defences, and 737 already names the fort as part of the land.

note: Both use Anni's cutting of Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai: 45 measures the gossip by the bards' clamour that day, 145 wishes on the foster mother's hand the fate of that felled tree.
teaches: One puram event served akam poets in two opposite ways, as a measure of noise and as a curse of destruction, which shows these battles were a shared stock of reference the audience was expected to know.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why anyone stays unlearned; 192 says every town is ours and everyone our kin, with no condition of learning.
teaches: The Kural makes belonging everywhere a reward of learning, while Kaniyan makes it a consequence of seeing that good and ill are not given by others, so the pair shows the same cosmopolitan claim earned once by study and once by insight.

note: Kural 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than the poverty of the good; 197 says the poet thinks nothing of the riches of the unfeeling and thinks of the poverty of the wise with joy.
teaches: The Kural's comparison is spoken by a poet to a Chola king's face in the Purananuru, which shows that the maxim's ranking of the wise poor over the ignorant rich was first a bard's claim on his own dignity before a patron.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

note: Both use the battle at Venni: in 246 the uproar of Karikalan's victory measures the town's gossip, in 55 the defeated Chera's death measures a mother's grief.
teaches: One battle gave akam poets images from both sides, the victor's clamour for gossip and the loser's death for grief, so a puram event's meaning in akam depends on whose side the image is taken from.

note: Kural 542 sets the world's dependence on the sky beside the people's dependence on the sceptre; 186 denies rice and water the name of life and gives it to the king alone.
teaches: The Kural keeps rain and rule as parallel supports, but Mosikeeranar ranks the king above food and water and then turns the claim into the king's own duty to know it, so the pair shows the same dependence read once as praise and once as a burden laid on the ruler.

note: Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and let us feast at home in the evening; Akananuru 44 opens with the king's work done and the tribute paid, and bids the chariot race home to sleep on her breast.
teaches: The Kural's couplet is the akam homecoming formula of the returning warrior reduced to its two clauses, the king's victory first and the household's evening second.

note: Kural 552 calls the sceptre-holder's demand a robber's demand at spear-point; 184 likens the greedy king to an elephant loose in a field.
teaches: The Kural condemns excess levy from the subject's side as robbery, while Pisirandhaiyar argues from the king's side that grabbing wastes more than it yields and leaves the king himself unfed, so the same rule is given both a moral and a prudential ground.

note: Both name Chezhiyan's attack on Musiri, the Chera port: 149 has him seize an image there, 57 compares the wife's suffering to the wounded in that clamorous siege.
teaches: Two separate paalai poems witness the same Pandya assault on Musiri, which shows a single war entering the akam repertoire as a ready image of suffering and plunder.

note: Kural 223 counts not saying 'I have nothing' and giving as the mark of the well-born; in 53 that very inability to refuse the needy is what drives the man away from the heroine.
teaches: The Kural's praise of giving has a cost the Kural does not count: in akam the generous man's virtue is the cause of the woman's abandonment.

note: Both give the man's reason for parting as the pursuit of glory or strength (நல்லிசை, உரன்), which takes his resolve as companion instead of her.
teaches: The friend's argument that glory is not for those who stay home is the very reason the Kural's woman lives on in longing, so the same heroic value comforts in one poem and wounds in the other.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Kural 1138 says love breaks through secrecy into the public square whatever the lover's restraint; in 52 the heroine, her pallor already visible, still forbids her friend to name it even at the cost of her life.
teaches: The Kural's rule that love cannot be hidden is qualified by the Sangam heroine's will: the body discloses it, but the naming is still hers to refuse.

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the new wife he has brought home

pairs.situation: he breaks the bond of his household
he does it secretly, while the town sleeps
the household is thrown into disorder

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a buffalo of the marutham fields in a marutham poem, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: at lamp-lighting the red-legged male dove calls to its beloved mate in the tall house
iraicchi.sense: at the hour when even the dove calls its mate home, the husband's absence is felt most, and his return is owed

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant bends the tall yaa tree with his head so that his young mate can eat its shoots, and fans the bees from his cheek
iraicchi.sense: on the very road the man took, the male feeds his mate, so he too will remember and come back to care for her

iraicchi.act: the young doe, tired of browsing, frolics unharmed in the joy of joining the stag
iraicchi.sense: the wife's release at his return will be as glad and as safe as the doe's play with her mate

iraicchi.act: the male vulture, its wings scorched, stays on the burning tree looking at the face of its hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even the vulture in the fire does not leave its mate, which is the choice the man makes against his heart

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant, worn by the summer heat, goes into the flood to bathe together with her bull
iraicchi.sense: the rains bring the parted together, and the man who has stayed to hold his wife is doing what the elephants do

iraicchi.act: at dusk the milch cows, udders full, hurry lowing to the homes where their tethered calves wait
iraicchi.sense: the man's return at the same hour is the cattle's return to their young: he goes home to his wife and son

note: 182 opens its catalogue with not eating alone even the nectar of the gods; Kural 322 makes sharing one's food the chief of all virtues.
teaches: Sharing food heads the list in both books, which shows that in early Tamil ethics the shared meal, not an inner disposition, was the first test of a good person.

note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

note: In both a cry of 'tiger' on the vengai slope brings men running: in 48 the girls' cry brings the young hunter who becomes the lover, in 52 a hill girl's cry for flowers brings the hill men with bows.
teaches: Together they show the vengai-plucking cry as a known custom of the hill, and 48 turns that public alarm into the private occasion of a first meeting that 52's heroine now wants kept secret.

note: Both have the returning man wish to finish the work and reach home for the evening; the Kural's evening feast at home is the poem's dusk arrival when the wife loosens her braid.
teaches: The Kural states as a wish what the mullai poem stages as a drive at dusk, showing that the evening return was the fixed goal of the man's speech in both traditions.

note: Both set a wedding drum against a funeral drum. Naladiyar 23 draws the lesson that the worthy hold to the way of escape; 194 tells those who know the world's nature to look for what is sweet (இனிய காண்க). On the reading that இனிய means good deeds in this life, the two conclusions diverge.
teaches: The same sight of joy and mourning side by side leads the Naladiyar to renunciation and the Purananuru poet to seeking good within the world, which shows the later didactic book reusing a Sangam image for a different, ascetic conclusion.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who accept good when it comes grieve when it does not; 192 neither rejoices that life is sweet nor calls it bitter, because a life follows its order.
teaches: Both ground equanimity on an order the person does not control, but the Kural names it ஊழ் and argues, while Kaniyan gives the picture of a raft carried on a flood, so the abstract fate of the Kural is given an image of how it works.

note: Both use the Kazhar legend of Aathi Manthi and Attan Atthi; 222 names Maruthi, who restored the lover and entered the sea, 236 has Manthi searching town after town.
teaches: One legend served two speakers: the friend holds up Maruthi's fatal deed as a fame to win, the wife holds up Manthi's lament as her own shame, so the story was a shared stock the poets bent to opposite purposes.

note: 189 says the use of wealth is giving and whoever means to enjoy it alone loses much; Naladiyar 9 says the man who neither eats, gives nor relieves his kin but guards his wealth is counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Both declare kept wealth already lost, but for different reasons: Nakkeerar from the fixed measure one body can eat and wear, the Naladiyar from the miser's failure in every use, so the pair gives the conclusion one ground in the body and one in duty.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: In 43 the man calls leaving a companion for wealth folly (மடமை) and pities those who do it; in 53 the heroine says her man left because his heart could not refuse the needy, a virtue she still reads as love of wealth over her.
teaches: Read together they show the paalai debate from both sides: the same departure is folly to one man and an unrefusable duty of giving to another, and the woman left behind refuses to call either grace.

note: Naladiyar 206 says saltless millet gruel among one's own is sweeter than milk rice from strangers' hands; 197 prizes the small chief's greens and varagu rice given with regard over kings' wealth.
teaches: Both value a poor meal for the regard it is given with, but the Naladiyar finds that regard among kin while the Purananuru finds it in a patron who knows a poet's worth, so the pair shows the bard's patron standing where the family stands in the later book.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: Both tell of Cheralathan, ashamed of his back wound from the fight with Karikalan, sitting facing north to die; Purananuru 65 laments the king, Akananuru 55 turns to the noble men who died with him.
teaches: The akam poem keeps a detail the puram lament leaves out, the companions who followed the king into death, and uses it to measure a mother's wish that her life would follow her daughter.

note: 194 declares இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம், this world is harsh, and blames its maker; 192 says we do not in disgust call life bitter (இன்னாது என்றலும் இலமே). Read as judgments of the world, they are incompatible.
teaches: One anthology holds both the verdict that the world is bitter and the refusal to pass that verdict, using the same word இன்னாது, so the reader sees that Purananuru ethics offered two stances to grief, protest and equanimity, rather than one doctrine.

note: Both liken a woman's bangle to a rich king's town (Chezhiyan's Allur in 46, Pazhaiyan's Por in 186), one from the wife's side and one from the courtesan's.
teaches: The town-like bangle is a shared formula that both rivals in the marutham triangle could use, so the formula marks a woman's claim on the man, not which side she is on.

note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.

note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the death rattle stops the tongue; 195, facing old men who have done no good, asks at least that they refrain from harm.
teaches: The Kural's urgency assumes one can still act well, while the Purananuru poet sets a floor for those who will not, so the pair shows that early Tamil counsel allowed abstaining from harm to count as a road to the good when doing good had failed.

note: Both set the absent man's wellbeing above the woman's pallor: the friend's blessing நோய்இலராக, the Kural's 'let my body pale, if he is well'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into the woman's own mouth a blessing that the Akananuru gives to the friend, showing how the anthology's go-between voice was absorbed into the single speaker of the later couplets.

note: Both measure gossip against a public spectacle: the Kural against the serpent swallowing the moon, the Akananuru against the shout at Katti's flight.
teaches: The Kural keeps the old akam habit of sizing a private scandal by a famous public event, but trades the historical rout for a cosmic eclipse, losing the political sting while keeping the scale.

note: 784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship.
teaches: The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

note: 475 says a light load breaks the axle when there is too much of it (அப்பண்டம் சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்).
teaches: Parimelazhagar takes the verse as an indirect statement that a strong king who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength when they combine. 873 says this outright: one who, alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more foolish than the mad.

note: Both refuse the promise of a quick return: the girl quotes his 'we will come right away' against the spring, the Kural says tell your quick return to those who will be alive.
teaches: Read together they show the same refusal of comfort in two registers, the Kural as a sharp retort before parting and the Akananuru as proof gathered afterwards from the season's signs.

note: 182 opens உண்டால் அம்ம, இவ்வுலகம் (the world exists, indeed) and 194 says இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம் (the world is harsh, indeed): the same exclamation over the same world.
teaches: Two poets use one formula to say opposite things about this world, and each turns it to action, so the formula shows the anthology arguing with itself: the world is kept going by the selfless in 182, and is bitter yet must be met by seeking good in 194.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Akananuru 54 calls Pannan தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்.
teaches: The kaanchi poem's general ideal and the akam poem's praise of one patron use the same contrast of self and others, so the maxim was already a phrase of praise for real patrons.

note: Kural 737 defines a country by its limbs: waters, a well-placed hill, the water from it and a strong fort. 187 says no kind of ground, plain, forest, low or high, makes a land good, only the goodness of its men. On the reading that both answer what makes a land good, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the land lists natural and built assets, while Avvaiyar dismisses terrain altogether, so a reader sees two answers to one question, resources or people, and that the Purananuru gave the moral answer before the treatise gave the material one.

note: Pannan of Sirukudi is praised in Purananuru 173 as the healer of hunger whose house feeds crowds; in Akananuru 54 his village's gooseberry gives the simile and he is called one who lives not for himself but for others.
teaches: An akam poet could fold a puram patron's reputation into one epithet inside a love poem, which shows how well-known Pannan's generosity was.

note: 399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent.
teaches: It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.

note: Both liken the beloved's coming to rain on those who live by it: the Kural states it as a rule of lovers' grace, Akananuru 42 makes it a drought broken at dawn over a whole countryside.
teaches: The Kural's two-line rain simile is the compressed form of a scene the Sangam poet builds at length, so the couplet's image carries the whole drought-and-tank picture behind it.

note: Kural 1155 says if he leaves, union becomes hard (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு); in 51 the man tells his heart that wealth is joined only by parting, and chooses to stay.
teaches: The same word புணர்வு carries both sides of one exchange: the Kural's woman counts what parting costs union, and the Sangam man counts what union costs wealth.

note: Both marutham poems reproach the husband for bathing in the Kaveri flood with the woman he desires (நீ வெய் யோளொடு), and both place it at Matthi's Kazhar near Thithan's Uranthai.
teaches: The shared phrase and places show that the bathing scandal at Kazhar was a set situation of marutham, which each poet then sharpened with a different puram comparison, a rout in 226 and a lost youth in 6.

note: Both rank learning above birth: in 183 a man of the highest order defers to a learned man of the lowest, and Kural 409 says the unlearned high-born lack the worth of the learned low-born.
teaches: The Kural's maxim was already a king's teaching in the Purananuru, where Nedunchezhiyan keeps the four orders by name and lets learning reverse them, so neither text abolishes birth rank: both use it as the measure that learning overturns.

iraicchi.act: the tiger goes out at midnight to bring prey to his mate, weak and hungry after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who comes by night should, like the tiger, take on the care of the woman rather than leave her

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his new brides

pairs.situation: he comes home bearing their marks

iraicchi.sense: the wife, left alone, remembers the full days together and finds them gone
